meta.scope: Fluent 2 on native platforms: iOS (fluentui-apple), Android (fluentui-android), Windows (WinUI 3 / WinUI 2 / WPF Fluent theme).
readThisFirst: Windows: WinUI 3 (Windows App SDK 2.4.0, released 2026-08-13) is current. WinUI 2 (Microsoft.UI.Xaml 2.8.7) is maintenance-only - last feature release 2.8, July 2022.
iOS has NO v8/v9-style split: one package, one product, one 0.x line; Fluent 2 is a version cutover at 0.13.0.
Android ships Fluent 1 (View/XML) and Fluent 2 (Jetpack Compose) inside the SAME artifacts, split by Kotlin package.
Pick the framework kind before generating code: uikit vs swiftui, view vs compose, winui3 vs winui2 vs wpf. Mixing them produces code that cannot compile.

ios.label: iOS - Fluent UI Apple (fluentui-apple)
ios.generationStory: iOS is ONE evolving line, not a v8/v9 split. The same pod (MicrosoftFluentUI) and the same SPM product (FluentUI) carry both generations; Fluent 2 is a version cutover at 0.13.0, which deleted Colors.swift and moved ColorProviding onto brand tokens. Legacy Fluent-1-era controls (CardView, DateTimePicker, PersonaListView) are still shipped in the same package.

frameworkKinds.meaning: SwiftUI View structs, e.g. Avatar, FluentList, ListItem. Style native SwiftUI.Button with FluentButtonStyle - there is no SwiftUI Fluent Button view.
UIKit classes (UIView/UIViewController subclasses), e.g. Button, SearchBar, DrawerController. MSF-prefixed types are ControlHostingView wrappers around SwiftUI controls.

generations.note: MS*-prefixed classes, Colors.primary API, iOS 11+, Carthage supported. No releases after 2020-04-17.
Rename only; still Fluent 1 design. Colors.swift + ColorProviding.primaryColor(for:) still present at 0.12.0.
Same pod and same product name, evolving in place. 0.13.0 deleted Colors.swift and switched ColorProviding to brand tokens.

theming.brandColor: Conform a type to ColorProviding (18 required brand properties: brandBackground1/1Pressed/1Selected/2/2Pressed/2Selected/3/Tint/Disabled, brandForeground1/1Pressed/1Selected/Tint/Disabled1/Disabled2, brandStroke1/1Pressed/1Selected; plus optional brandGradient1/2/3). Apply app-wide with FluentTheme.setSharedThemeColorProvider(provider), or per view-hierarchy with someView.setColorProvider(provider). SwiftUI: build a FluentTheme(colorOverrides:) and apply .fluentTheme(theme).
theming.darkMode: Every alias color is a DynamicColor with light/dark/darkElevated slots resolved by UITraitCollection; no manual dark-mode switch. visionOS collapses brand overrides to the light value only.
theming.highContrast: No accessibilityContrast handling was found on main; DynamicColor has only light/dark/darkElevated (0.11.0 had lightHighContrast/darkHighContrast). Negative finding - see unverified.

typographyNotes.fontFamily: Apple system font; the ramp snaps to Apple system point sizes, not web px.
typographyNotes.webEquivalentCaveat: Slot names match web Fluent 2, numeric values do not. Web-side names were not re-verified this pass.

accessibility.screenReader: Controls ship localized VoiceOver strings in Sources/FluentUI_iOS/Resources/Localization/<lang>.lproj/Localizable.strings - VERIFIED 36 locales at tag 0.37.0 (36 *.lproj directories; the frequently repeated "~40" was never sourced). Examples: Accessibility.ActivityIndicator.Animating.label, Accessibility.AvatarView.LabelFormat, Presence.OOF. Most controls expose an overridable accessibilityLabel on their state object.
accessibility.dynamicType: Label sets adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true and observes UIContentSizeCategory.didChangeNotification; Label.maxFontSize caps growth. theme.typography(_:adjustsForContentSizeCategory:) lets a token opt out (Avatar and SegmentedControl pass false).
accessibility.touchTargets: No global minimum-target API found. Button sizing comes from ButtonTokenSet.minContainerHeight(style:size:); Fluent defers to Apple HIG otherwise.
providedAutomatically: Localized VoiceOver labels for ActivityIndicator, ProgressBar, Avatar (incl. out-of-office)
Traits: .isImage on ActivityIndicator, .updatesFrequently on ProgressBar
Determinate ProgressBar exposes accessibilityValue as a percent string
Large Content Viewer via .showsLargeContentViewer(...) and UILargeContentViewerInteraction
Keyboard/pointer focus ring drawn by SegmentedControl; pointerInteraction on Fluent buttons
DEBUG-only descriptive accessibilityIdentifiers for UI test automation
Dark/darkElevated color variants resolved automatically per trait collection
notProvided: High-contrast token set (no accessibilityContrast handling found)
A global minimum touch-target enforcement API
accessibility.designGuidance: Fluent iOS is a customized subset that fits alongside native Apple components; iOS pages defer to Apple HIG for determinate progress bars and text views.

android.label: Android - Fluent UI Android (fluentui-android)
android.generationStory: Android DOES have two generations, but they ship inside the SAME Maven artifacts, separated by Kotlin package. Fluent 1 = View-based (XML), package com.microsoft.fluentui.<area>.*, feature-frozen. Fluent 2 = Jetpack Compose, package com.microsoft.fluentui.tokenized.*, actively developed. Adding the umbrella artifact pulls in both - the package you import decides which generation you get.

frameworkKinds.meaning: Fluent 2. @Composable functions under com.microsoft.fluentui.tokenized.*. Requires Compose enabled in the consuming module.
Fluent 1. Android View subclasses used from XML layouts, under com.microsoft.fluentui.<area>.*. Still published and compiled; no @Deprecated found.

tokens.system: Three layers in fluentui_core: FluentGlobalTokens (primitives) -> AliasTokens/IAliasTokens (semantic, keyed by FluentAliasTokens enums) -> ControlTokens (per-control). FluentTheme supplies all three via CompositionLocals.
tokens.namingWarning: Object is FluentGlobalTokens, NOT GlobalTokens. Keys live on FluentAliasTokens; values on the overridable class AliasTokens.
tokens.tokenSetApi: class TokenSet<T,V>(defaultValues:(T)->V) { operator fun get(t:T):V; operator fun set(k:T,v:V) } - per-key override or subclass-and-override.
tokens.gotcha: If explicit aliasTokens/controlTokens are passed to FluentTheme(...), runtime FluentTheme.updateXxx() will NOT affect that scope.

theming.brandColor: Subclass AliasTokens and override brandColor (16 BrandColorTokens steps), falling back to super.brandColor[token]. BrandBackground/Foreground/Stroke derive from it automatically.
theming.darkMode: enum ThemeMode { Light, Dark, Auto }. Auto (default) follows isSystemInDarkTheme(). Resolved in FluentColor.value()/FluentIcon.value(). Set via FluentTheme(themeMode=) or FluentTheme.updateThemeMode().
theming.highContrast: NO SUPPORT FOUND. A repo-wide search for highContrast / isHighTextContrastEnabled / HighContrast returned 0 results; no HC token set or detection exists. Phrase this as "none found", not "Microsoft does not support it".
theming.fluentStyle: FluentStyle { Neutral, Brand } is an orthogonal per-control surface style used by AppBar, SearchBar, PillButton, TabItem, progress indicators.
theming.shippedExamples: Demo app has OneNoteAliasTokens, WordAliasTokens, ExcelAliasTokens, PowerPointAliasTokens, TeamsAliasTokens, M365AliasTokens.
theming.entryPoint: @Composable fun FluentTheme(aliasTokens: IAliasTokens? = null, controlTokens: IControlTokens? = null, themeMode: ThemeMode? = null, content: @Composable () -> Unit)

typographyNotes.missingSlots: Android has no Subtitle1/Subtitle2; it uses '...Strong' variants instead.

color.sharedColorSets: 30+ named ramps (Anchor, Beige, Berry, Blue, Brass, Bronze, Brown, Burgundy, Charcoal, Cornflower, Cranberry, Cyan, DarkBlue, DarkGreen, DarkOrange, Red, Green, Yellow, Orange, Marigold, ...) each with primary + shade10-50 + tint10-60.
color.webComparison: Brand ramp and neutral greys are IDENTICAL to web Fluent 2 (Color80 #0F6CBD, Grey14 #242424). Differences: Caption1 13sp vs 12px, Caption2 12sp vs 10px, Title1 Bold 700 vs Semibold 600, no Segoe UI font family, no Subtitle1/2 slots.

accessibility.screenReader: TalkBack: controls set correct Compose Roles (Button/Checkbox/RadioButton/Switch); Avatar merges descendants into one description; Drawer and BottomSheet announce state changes via announceForAccessibility with overridable strings.
accessibility.touchTargets: NOT handled automatically. Repo-wide search for minimumInteractiveComponentSize/minimumTouchTargetSize returned 0 results. CheckBox ripple is 48dp but the hit target is not expanded - callers must add padding/sizeIn to reach Material's 48x48dp minimum.

A repo-wide search for highContrast / isHighTextContrastEnabled / HighContrast returned 0 results, and no HC token set, theme or detection exists in the codebase. This is strong negative evidence from a search, not a Microsoft statement of non-support.

windows.label: Windows - WinUI 3 (Windows App SDK), WinUI 2 (UWP), WPF Fluent theme
windows.generationStory: Windows has three live stacks. WinUI 3 ships inside the Windows App SDK (Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK 2.4.0) and is the recommended framework for new Windows desktop apps. WinUI 2 (Microsoft.UI.Xaml 2.8.7, UWP) is MAINTENANCE ONLY - its last feature release was WinUI 2.8 in July 2022; 2.8.7 is a servicing patch. WPF got an official Fluent theme in .NET 9 (assembly PresentationFramework.Fluent) that restyles existing WPF controls - it adds no new control set. WinUI 2.6 (June 2021) was the Fluent 2 inflection point on Windows (Mica, Windows 11 visual styles).
windows.maintenanceWarning: Do NOT start a new app on WinUI 2. It has had no feature release since July 2022 and exists to serve UWP (Xbox, HoloLens, IoT), which the Windows App SDK does not support.
windows.sourceBranches: microsoft/microsoft-ui-xaml default branch is 'main'; the active WinUI 3 branch is 'winui3/main' and WinUI 2 lives on 'winui2/main'. WinUI 3 theme resources are under controls/dev/CommonStyles/ (WinUI 2: dev/CommonStyles/).

frameworkKinds.meaning: Current. Win32 desktop, Windows 10 1809 (17763)+, shipped in Microsoft.WindowsAppSDK. Namespace Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Controls.

Maintenance only. UWP, Windows 10 1809+, shipped in Microsoft.UI.Xaml 2.8.7. Use only for Xbox, HoloLens or IoT. Controls carry the same type names and the Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Controls namespace, but the UWP XAML namespace mapping was not verified - check whether a prefix is required before emitting WinUI 2 XAML.
WPF Fluent theme (.NET 9+). Restyles built-in WPF controls via PresentationFramework.Fluent; no new controls.

generations.artifact: Fluent Design System (Project NEON) - Reveal, Acrylic, Parallax, Connected Animations
generations.note: Only Acrylic survives in current Learn guidance. Reveal has no live Learn page - see unverified.
2.6 (Jun 2021) added Mica + Windows 11 visual styles. 2.8 was the final feature release.

WASDK 2.4.0 shipped 13 Aug 2026 (GitHub release v2.4.0, prerelease=false); 1.8.11, published the same day, is the current 1.8 servicing release. WASDK 2.0 is the Current channel (end of servicing 04/29/2027); 1.8 is Maintenance until 09/09/2026.
Official Microsoft. .NET 10 added Fluent styling for DatePicker, GridSplitter, GridView, GroupBox, Hyperlink, Label, NavigationWindow, RichTextBox, TextBox.

This was verified for WinUI 3 only - the UWP/WinUI 2 namespace mapping was not verified this pass, so do not assume the same for WinUI 2.

tokens.system: XAML theme resources, not CSS-style tokens. Every semantic token exists as a Color (e.g. TextFillColorPrimary) AND a matching SolidColorBrush (TextFillColorPrimaryBrush), defined in three theme dictionaries keyed Default (= Dark), Light and HighContrast.

markupExtensions.ThemeResource: Re-evaluated at app load AND on every runtime theme change. Use in Styles, Setters, control templates, property setters, animations.
markupExtensions.StaticResource: Evaluated once at load. Use INSIDE ThemeDictionaries.
markupExtensions.exception: Inside ThemeDictionaries you may use {ThemeResource} for theme-agnostic system resources (SystemAccentColor, SystemColor*).
markupExtensions.commonBug: Getting these backwards is the #1 theming bug; it also causes brush-sharing pollution across sub-trees with different RequestedTheme.

tokens.notStaticColors: AccentTextFillColorPrimary/Secondary/TertiaryBrush are NOT static colors - they bind to SystemAccentColorDark2/Dark3/Dark1 in Light theme and SystemAccentColorLight3/Light3/Light2 in Dark theme. SystemFillColorAttentionBrush binds to SystemAccentColor (Light) / SystemAccentColorLight2 (Dark).

elevationBorderBrushes.note: LinearGradientBrush resources, not SolidColorBrush - they draw Fluent 2's subtle bottom-edge highlight.
elevationBorderBrushes.sample:
<LinearGradientBrush x:Key="ControlElevationBorderBrush" MappingMode="Absolute" StartPoint="0,0" EndPoint="0,3">
  <GradientStop Offset="0.33" Color="{StaticResource ControlStrokeColorSecondary}"/>
  <GradientStop Offset="1.0"  Color="{StaticResource ControlStrokeColorDefault}"/>
</LinearGradientBrush>
elevationBorderBrushes.gotcha: The Light dictionary adds a ScaleTransform ScaleY="-1" RelativeTransform that the Dark dictionary omits.

cornerRadius.note: Only TWO global radius tokens exist, identical in Light, Dark and HighContrast.
cornerRadius.designIntent: 8px top-level containers (windows, flyouts, dialogs); 4px in-page and bar elements (Button, CheckBox, ComboBox, TextBox, ListView, ProgressBar, ScrollBar, Slider); 0px where straight edges meet (SplitButton halves, flyout-to-anchor edge, snapped/maximized windows). ToolTip is an exception at 4px.
cornerRadius.count: EXACTLY TWO - VERIFIED at controls/dev/CommonStyles/CornerRadius_themeresources.xaml (winui3/main): ControlCornerRadius (4,4,4,4) and OverlayCornerRadius (8,8,8,8), repeated identically in the Default, Light and HighContrast theme dictionaries. Everything else in that file is a CornerRadiusFilterConverter/CornerRadiusToThicknessConverter, not a token. Windows has no per-size radius ramp the way the web tokens do.

elevation.warning: These elevation numbers are DESIGN tokens, not XAML resource keys. There is no ElevationCardShadow-style resource - use ThemeShadow or a Composition DropShadow.

lightweightStyling.note: Per-control token keys follow <ControlName><Part>[<State>], e.g. ButtonBackground, ButtonForeground, ButtonBorderBrush + ...PointerOver / ...Pressed / ...Disabled.
lightweightStyling.guidance: Prefer lightweight styling over re-templating. If you must derive a Style, base it on Default<ControlName>Style (DefaultTextBoxStyle, DefaultContentDialogStyle) - but omit BasedOn for WinUI controls whose default style lives in metadata.

theming.themes: Three: Light, Dark, HighContrast. Removing RequestedTheme = follow the user's Windows setting, which is the correct default. A user-selected contrast theme OVERRIDES your RequestedTheme.
theming.requestedTheme: <Application x:Class="App9.App" RequestedTheme="Dark"/> - RequestedTheme also exists on FrameworkElement for sub-tree theming, but that triggers brush-sharing pollution. Always supply explicit Light AND Dark dictionaries rather than a single Default.
theming.accentColor: SystemAccentColor resolves at runtime to the user's Windows personalization accent. Shell palette: SystemAccentColorLight3/Light2/Light1, SystemAccentColor, SystemAccentColorDark1/Dark2/Dark3. Programmatic: UISettings.GetColorValue(UIColorType).

highContrast.builtInThemes: Aquatic, Desert, Dusk, Night sky (Settings > Accessibility > Contrast themes; Left Alt + Left Shift + PrtScn defaults to Aquatic). Contrast ratios typically >= 7:1.

systemColorKeys.use: Headings, body, lists, placeholders, borders, non-interactive UI
Background of selected, hovered, pressed, in-progress UI

highContrast.tripwire: WinUI deliberately defines SystemColorWindowTextColorBrush et al. as magenta #FF00FF in the Light/Dark dictionaries. Magenta on screen means you used a HighContrast-only key in the wrong theme.
highContrast.sample:
<ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>
  <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Light">
    <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BrandedPageBackgroundBrush" Color="#E6E6E6"/>
  </ResourceDictionary>
  <ResourceDictionary x:Key="Dark">
    <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BrandedPageBackgroundBrush" Color="#1F1F1F"/>
  </ResourceDictionary>
  <ResourceDictionary x:Key="HighContrast">
    <SolidColorBrush x:Key="BrandedPageBackgroundBrush" Color="{ThemeResource SystemColorWindowColor}"/>
  </ResourceDictionary>
</ResourceDictionary.ThemeDictionaries>

theming.wpf: WPF: prefer ThemeMode (Light | Dark | System | None). Setting it in code is experimental and raises WPF0001 - suppress with <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);WPF0001</NoWarn>. Accent colors come from System.Windows.SystemColors and MUST be bound with DynamicResource.

typographyNotes.font: Segoe UI Variable (download: https://aka.ms/SegoeUIVariable). Axes: wght Thin 100 -> Bold 700 (Light 300, Semilight 350, Regular 400, Semibold 600, Bold 700) and opsz, which is automatic and on by default in XAML from 8pt to 36pt.
typographyNotes.baseStyle: BaseTextBlockStyle sets FontFamily=XamlAutoFontFamily, FontWeight=SemiBold, FontSize={StaticResource BodyTextBlockFontSize}, TextTrimming=CharacterEllipsis, TextWrapping=Wrap, LineStackingStrategy=MaxHeight, TextLineBounds=Full. Everything >=18px also sets OpticalMarginAlignment=TrimSideBearings.
rules: Sentence case for all UI text, including titles.
No Bold and no Italic in the Windows ramp - use Semibold for emphasis (italic hurts readability for dyslexic readers).
Left-align by default; centre only rarely (e.g. text under icons).
50-60 characters per line; never below 20 or above 60.
Sizes are effective pixels (epx); the scaling system handles DPI - do not adjust per screen size.
typographyNotes.icons: Segoe Fluent Icons (Windows 11 default; replaced Segoe MDL2 Assets). Monoline 1 epx stroke. Optimal sizes 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64 - off-ramp sizes render blurry. E0-E5 prefixed glyphs are deprecated legacy. Not present on Windows 10 by default.
typographyNotes.nonLatin: Segoe UI Variable covers English, European, Greek, Russian. Otherwise Ebrima, Gadugi, Leelawadee UI, Malgun Gothic, Microsoft JhengHei UI, Microsoft YaHei UI, Myanmar Text, Nirmala UI, Segoe UI (Arabic/Armenian/Georgian/Hebrew), Yu Gothic UI. Mapping via Windows.Globalization.Fonts.LanguageFont. Selawik is the open-source metric-compatible Segoe UI substitute.
typographyNotes.vsWeb: Windows uses XAML Style keys + x:Double size keys and epx with automatic optical sizing; web Fluent 2 uses CSS custom properties (--fontSizeBase300), px/rem and manual optical sizing. The numeric ladders differ - do not assume a 1:1 mapping.

set.name: Mica
set.type: Occluding, opaque; samples the desktop wallpaper once
set.use: Base layer of long-lived windows. Prioritise visibility in the title bar.

set.name: Mica Alt
set.type: Mica variant with a stronger wallpaper tint
set.use: Base layer when the title bar and commanding areas need contrast - canonical case is a tabbed title bar. Requires WASDK 1.1+ on Windows 11 22000+.

set.name: Acrylic
set.type: Semi-transparent frosted glass; recipe is background -> blur -> exclusion blend -> tint overlay -> noise
set.use: TRANSIENT, light-dismiss surfaces only - flyouts, context menus, non-modal popups.
set.fallback: Solid fallback color when transparency is off

set.name: Smoke
set.use: Dims content behind a modal dialog.

set.name: Reveal highlight
set.use: Removed from current Windows design guidance; not part of Fluent 2 on Windows.

materials.fallbackTriggers: Transparency effects off in Settings > Personalization > Color; Battery Saver; low-end hardware; window deactivated (background acrylic / Mica); Windows build < 22000 (Mica). High Contrast always wins.
materials.applying: Declarative Window.SystemBackdrop (WASDK 1.3+) is the recommended path. Elements exposing SystemBackdrop: Window, FlyoutBase, MenuFlyoutPresenter, Popup, CommandBarFlyoutCommandBar, DesktopWindowXamlSource, ContentIsland.
materials.controllers: Advanced: MicaController / DesktopAcrylicController (Microsoft.UI.Composition.SystemBackdrops), both ISystemBackdropController. Need MicaController.IsSupported(), an ICompositionSupportsSystemBackdrop target, a SystemBackdropConfiguration and DispatcherQueue.EnsureSystemDispatcherQueue(). Setting TintColor, TintOpacity, LuminosityOpacity or FallbackColor STOPS auto-update on theme change.
layeringRules: Mica (2 layers): Mica base -> content layer using LayerFillColorDefaultBrush.
Mica Alt (3 layers): Mica Alt base -> commanding layer using LayerOnMicaBaseAltFillColorDefaultBrush -> content layer using LayerFillColorDefaultBrush.
DO set Background="Transparent" on every layer you want Mica to show through.
DON'T apply backdrop material more than once per app.
DON'T place accent-coloured text on acrylic (fails contrast at 14px) and avoid hyperlinks over acrylic.
DON'T put two acrylic panes edge to edge - the seam is visible.

accessibility.screenReader: Narrator is the built-in Windows screen reader (touch mode supported). It both announces the whole UI on app switch and announces per-control on tab focus. Not all screen readers support all automation properties - test with several. AccScope visualises your UI as an automation tree with a Narrator-focused view.
accessibility.foundation: UI Automation (UIA). Every control class has an AutomationPeer reporting role and content to UIA clients; the app is a top-level window to UIA.

Layout panels derive default tab order from layout order; ListView/GridView give arrow-key navigation

High contrast resolves to HighContrast theme resources automatically - provided you do not hard-code colors
AutomationControlType via the peer; value patterns where semantically meaningful (TextBox -> IValueProvider)

youMustDo.purpose: Accessible name. Do not repeat the role ('button button'). Required on Image.
Associate a visible label with an input. Preferred over duplicating strings.
Accessible description; Narrator reads on demand via CapsLock+F.
Move noisy composed nodes to Raw so they leave the control/content views.
Enabled by default, forcing white-on-black text. Set to None if you already use system-aware brushes.
Required for custom controls; a dedicated peer is usually correct.

A layout container. Arranges children; renders no chrome of its own.
A Brush you assign to a Fill/Background/Foreground - not an element.
A SystemBackdrop applied to a window or element; has no visual tree presence itself.
A Shadow object assigned to UIElement.Shadow.
An IconElement used as the content of another control.
An ICommand object supplying label, icon, accelerator and description.
A property on Application/Window, not a type you instantiate.
A shipped assembly / resource dictionary, not an API.
A ResourceKey to look up with DynamicResource - not a type.

winui2Comparison.method: Directory diff of controls/dev/ on branch winui3/main against dev/ on branch winui2/main (GitHub git/trees?recursive=1), plus the [MUX_*] gate on each IDL.
winui2Comparison.caveat: A directory existing on winui2/main does NOT mean the type shipped in a WinUI 2 package: WinUI 2.8 (July 2022) was the last feature release, and both TitleBar and ScrollView are gated MUX_EXPERIMENTAL / MUX_PREVIEW there. Trust the gate, not the directory.

sharedConcepts: Three-tier token system on every platform: global/primitive ramps -> semantic alias tokens -> per-control token sets. Windows expresses tier 3 as 'lightweight styling' resource keys.
Same brand ramp: 16 steps, brand 80 = #0F6CBD on web, iOS (comm80) and Android (Color80). Windows instead defers to the user's SystemAccentColor.
Same neutral grey ramp on iOS/Android/web (Grey14 #242424, Grey96 #F5F5F5).
Same shared status color ramps: blue #0078D4, cranberry/red #C50F1F, green #107C10, dark orange #DA3B01.

Same typography slot vocabulary on iOS/Android/web (display, largeTitle, title1-3, body1/2 (+Strong), caption1/2) - numeric values differ per platform. Windows uses its own ramp (Caption/Body/Body Large/Subtitle/Title/Title Large/Display).

Light and dark are first-class everywhere. High contrast is first-class only on Windows (HighContrast theme dictionary + SystemColor* keys); iOS has no accessibilityContrast handling and Android has none at all.
Every platform intentionally sits alongside its host system's design language: iOS with Apple HIG/native components, Android with Material, Windows via WinUI itself.

namingDifferences.windows: ControlCornerRadius (4) / OverlayCornerRadius (8) - only two keys exist
no token - stroke width 1 is a design value
no spacing token set - use Margin/Padding/Spacing values
Mica / Mica Alt / Acrylic system backdrops

crossPlatform.tokenParity: Partial, and strongest at the primitive layer. The brand ramp and neutral greys are literally identical across web, iOS and Android; the semantic alias layer shares NAMES but not spelling; the type ramp shares slot names but not numbers (iOS body1 = 17pt, Android Body1 = 16sp, web body1 = px). Windows is the outlier: it has its own token vocabulary (TextFillColor*, ControlFillColor*, SolidBackgroundFillColor*), derives brand from the user's SystemAccentColor rather than a fixed #0F6CBD ramp, exposes only two corner-radius tokens, and has no spacing token set at all. Never assume a token name from one platform exists on another - look it up.

generationSummary.web: Fluent 1 (v8, @fluentui/react) and Fluent 2 (v9, @fluentui/react-components) are separate packages that coexist. See the fluent_v8_lookup tool.
generationSummary.ios: ONE evolving line. Same pod and SPM product throughout; Fluent 2 is a version cutover at 0.13.0. No v8/v9-style split exists.
generationSummary.android: Two generations in the SAME artifacts: Fluent 1 = View/XML under com.microsoft.fluentui.<area>.*, Fluent 2 = Compose under com.microsoft.fluentui.tokenized.*.
generationSummary.windows: WinUI 3 (Windows App SDK 2.4.0) is current; WinUI 2 (Microsoft.UI.Xaml 2.8.7) is maintenance-only since July 2022; WPF has an official Fluent theme from .NET 9.

designSiteDoctrine: 'Natural on every platform' is design principle #1: reuse native platform components and patterns 80% of the time, focusing energy on signature experiences.
The Fluent 2 design language file houses global and alias styling variables - color, stroke width, corner radius, spacing and size tokens - for web AND mobile.
Fluent 2 Core UI Kits are described as code-aligned building blocks for web, iOS and Android. Windows is not in that tier list.
The /component-roadmap/ page is React v9 only - it has no iOS/Android/Windows rows, so it is not a cross-platform artifact.

siteRouteNotes.routeShape: The real native route shape is /components/{ios|android}/core/{name}/usage/ - NOT /components/{platform}/{name}. Windows and React Native have index pages only.
siteRouteNotes.brokenInPageLinks: Cross-links authored inside native pages omit /core/ (e.g. /components/ios/avatargroup/usage) and return the site 404 page. One link even uses a capital 'OS' (/components/iOS/shimmer/usage). Rewrite short links to insert /core/.
siteRouteNotes.previewTags: All 12 iOS component pages render a visible 'Preview' tag; all 5 Android pages suppress it. The site never states the policy in prose.
siteRouteNotes.sectionVocabulary: Native pages use only Resources, Types, Behavior, Layout, Accessibility, Content. There are no Anatomy/States/Variants sections and zero tables on any native page.
siteRouteNotes.windowsIsAStub: VERIFIED (2026-08-16): GET /components/windows/ returns 200. It is NOT missing - it is a stub: a single page with two link tiles (WinUI 3 Figma toolkit https://aka.ms/WinUI/3.0-figma-toolkit, WinUI 3 docs https://aka.ms/windev), no XAML type names and no per-control pages. Windows token data must come from Learn + the WinUI repo, not fluent2.microsoft.design.

whyOutOfScope: This dataset covers the three platform-native libraries - Swift/UIKit+SwiftUI, Kotlin/Compose+Views, and XAML. React Native is a JavaScript framework whose API shape follows the WEB Fluent conventions (props, style objects, tokens), not the native ones.

fluent2.microsoft.design has no usable React Native documentation: /components/react-native/ 302s to AAD sign-in, and React Native is absent from the site platform switcher (React / iOS / Android / Windows).
Emitting 25 half-grounded entries would dilute a dataset whose whole value is that every entry was read from source. A grounded pointer beats a padded list.
reactNative.whatToDoInstead: Read the component source under packages/components/<Name>/src in microsoft/fluentui-react-native, or use the web Fluent 2 tools (fluent_get_component / fluent_list_tokens) for the design language, which is shared. Do not translate the web React v9 API into React Native - the packages differ.
